# Benign and premalignant lesions of the endometrium

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Obstetrics/gynecology > Neoplastic disorders > Benign and premalignant lesions of the endometrium*

[Original Article Link](/library/UJ0btS)

---

## Summary

<u>Endometrial hyperplasia</u> is an abnormal <u>proliferation</u> of the <u>endometrium</u> caused by increased <u>estrogen</u> stimulation. It manifests with <u>abnormal uterine bleeding</u> (<u>AUB</u>) or <u>postmenopausal bleeding</u> (<u>PMB</u>) and is classified as <u>endometrial hyperplasia without atypia</u>, which is benign; and <u>endometrial hyperplasia with atypia</u> (<u>endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia</u>; <u>EIN</u>), which is premalignant. <u>Endometrial hyperplasia</u> is a histopathologic diagnosis based on <u>endometrial sampling</u> and <u>histopathology</u>. <u>Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia</u> is treated with <u>progestin</u> therapy (i.e., <u>levonorgestrel IUD</u> or oral <u>progestins</u>). Total <u>hysterectomy</u> is preferred for <u>EIN</u> because of the high risk of concurrent <u>endometrial cancer</u> or progression to <u>endometrial cancer</u>. <u>Progestin</u> therapy with close surveillance may be considered for patients who desire future <u>fertility</u>.




<u>Endometrial polyps</u> are localized overgrowths of <u>endometrial</u> tissue and mainly affect <u>postmenopausal</u> individuals. Though usually asymptomatic, <u>endometrial polyps</u> can cause abnormal <u>vaginal bleeding</u> and, in <u>premenopausal</u> individuals, <u>infertility</u>. Diagnosis is typically made with <u>transvaginal ultrasound</u> (<u>TVUS</u>) and/or <u>hysteroscopy</u>. Treatment involves <u>watchful waiting</u> in asymptomatic <u>premenopausal</u> patients and surgical removal in symptomatic <u>premenopausal</u> patients, all <u>postmenopausal</u> patients, and patients with <u>risk factors for malignant endometrial polyps</u>.

---

## Endometrial hyperplasia

* <u>Endometrial hyperplasia</u> is an abnormal thickening of the uterine lining caused by the <u>proliferation</u> of <u>endometrium</u> due to <u>estrogen</u> stimulation and insufficient <u>progestin</u> stimulation.

* <u>Risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia</u> are the same as <u>risk factors for type I endometrial cancer</u>. [[2]](/library/wNdhWq0)





### Clinical features




Abnormal <u>vaginal bleeding</u> is the defining symptom of <u>endometrial hyperplasia</u>. See:




* Clinical features of <u>AUB</u> (e.g., <u>intermenstrual bleeding</u>)

* <u>Postmenopausal bleeding</u> (<u>PMB</u>)





### Diagnosis [[2]](/library/wNdhWq0)[[3]](/library/GY1Bq20)




* The diagnostic workup for suspected <u>endometrial hyperplasia</u> follows the same approach as <u>diagnostics for endometrial cancer</u>.

* <u>Endometrial hyperplasia</u> is confirmed on <u>histopathology</u> findings of <u>endometrial sampling</u>; see “<u>Indications for endometrial sampling</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> <u>Endometrial hyperplasia</u> is a histopathologic diagnosis. <u>Endometrial sampling</u> should be performed in all patients (<u>postmenopausal</u> or of childbearing age) with abnormal <u>vaginal bleeding</u> and <u>risk factors for endometrial cancer</u> to evaluate for <u>EIN</u> or <u>endometrial cancer</u>. [[4]](/library/uEWpxM0)[[5]](/library/ce1aBf0)[[6]](/library/wldh_J0)




#### <u>Postmenopausal</u> individuals [[5]](/library/ce1aBf0)




* Patients with <u>PMB</u>

* <u>Endometrial</u> thickness > 4 mm on <u>TVUS</u> suggests <u>endometrial hyperplasia</u> or <u>endometrial cancer</u>.   [[3]](/library/GY1Bq20)[[5]](/library/ce1aBf0)[[7]](/library/dmdoeq0)[[8]](/library/3yWSUL0)

* Diagnosis is confirmed on <u>endometrial sampling</u> and <u>histopathology</u>.

* See “<u>Diagnostic workup for PMB</u>” for a detailed approach.

* Incidentally detected <u>endometrial</u> thickness > 4 mm (asymptomatic individuals)

* Routine evaluation is not required.

* Tailor further management based on <u>risk factors for endometrial cancer</u>.





![Endometrial thickening with cystic changes](media/vp00tko8b2n0pdvgmaz849pa.jpg)

Endometrial thickening with cystic changes




#### Reproductive-aged individuals




* <u>Endometrial</u> thickness alone is an unreliable indicator of an <u>endometrial</u> pathology.

* Diagnosis is confirmed on <u>endometrial sampling</u> performed as part of the <u>diagnostic workup for AUB</u>.





#### <u>Histopathology</u> findings




| <br>Classification of endometrial hyperplasia based on histology (WHO 2014) [[9]](/library/23bT3t)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br>Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia (<u>benign endometrial hyperplasia</u>) <br> | <br>Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia (<u>endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia</u>; <u>EIN</u>) <br> |
| <u>Histology</u> | <br><br>* Simple <u>endometrial</u> <u>proliferation</u> with a few cysts<br><br>* Enlarged, dilated <u>mucous membrane</u> glands (Swiss cheese pattern) located between abundant stromal tissue<br><br>* Lack of cytological <u>atypia</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Pronounced <u>proliferation</u> of <u>glandular tissue</u><br><br>* Glands are positioned back-to-back with no separating stroma<br><br>* Clonal, <u>atypical cells</u> with extensive <u>mitosis</u> and loss of cell polarity<br><br><br> |
| Risk of <u>carcinoma</u> | <br>* Low (1–3%)<br><br> | <br>* Very high risk of <u>endometrial carcinoma</u><br><br>* ∼ 30% risk of progression to <u>endometrial cancer</u> within a year [[2]](/library/wNdhWq0)<br><br>* Up to 50% of patients have concurrent invasive <u>endometrial cancer</u>. [[10]](/library/IOdYFJ0)[[11]](/library/CIdqUr0)[[12]](/library/V5bGQ8)<br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia</u> (<u>EIN</u>) is a precursor for <u>endometrial cancer</u>. <u>Endometrial intraepithelial carcinoma</u> (<u>EIC</u>) is a distinct entity and is a precursor for <u>papillary</u> serous uterine cancer. [[2]](/library/wNdhWq0)

### Differential diagnoses




* <u>Endometrial cancer</u> [[5]](/library/ce1aBf0)

* <u>Endometrial</u> <u>atrophy</u> [[5]](/library/ce1aBf0)

* Other <u>causes of AUB</u>

* Other <u>causes of PMB</u>





### Management [[2]](/library/wNdhWq0)[[10]](/library/IOdYFJ0)




* The choice of treatment depends on the presence of <u>atypia</u> and if future <u>fertility</u> is desired.

* In all patients, reversible causes of excess <u>estrogen</u> should be identified and treated.





#### <u>Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia</u> [[13]](/library/BNdzWq0)[[14]](/library/2odTYI0)[[15]](/library/nod7cI0)




* <u>Progestin</u> therapy

* Preferred management for all patients [[13]](/library/BNdzWq0)

* Options

* <u>Levonorgestrel IUD</u> (<u>off-label</u>) [[16]](/library/xNdEWq0)

* Continuous oral <u>progestins</u>, e.g., <u>medroxyprogesterone acetate</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[13]](/library/BNdzWq0)[[15]](/library/nod7cI0)

* Further management: Repeat <u>endometrial sampling</u> to assess treatment response after 3–6 months of treatment.  [[13]](/library/BNdzWq0)

* Surveillance with repeat <u>endometrial sampling</u>

* Indications

* Patients with <u>contraindications to progestins</u>

* Patient preference

* Spontaneous regression is seen in ∼ 75% of patients.  [[13]](/library/BNdzWq0)[[15]](/library/nod7cI0)

* Advise patients to promptly follow up with their treating physician if they experience abnormal <u>vaginal bleeding</u> during <u>conservative management</u>.





#### <u>Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia</u> (<u>EIN</u>) [[2]](/library/wNdhWq0)[[10]](/library/IOdYFJ0)[[17]](/library/DNd1Wq0)




Refer patients to gynecology or gynecologic oncology for evaluation and management.




* Total <u>hysterectomy</u> with or without bilateral <u>salpingo-oophorectomy</u> [[2]](/library/wNdhWq0)[[10]](/library/IOdYFJ0)

* Definitive management for <u>EIN</u>

* Indications

* All <u>postmenopausal</u> patients

* <u>Premenopausal</u> patients not desiring future <u>pregnancy</u>

* <u>Progestin</u> therapy with surveillance  [[2]](/library/wNdhWq0)[[10]](/library/IOdYFJ0)[[17]](/library/DNd1Wq0)

* Concurrent <u>endometrial cancer</u> must first be ruled out, preferably with hysteroscopic-guided <u>endometrial sampling</u>. [[10]](/library/IOdYFJ0)

* Indications

* Patients who cannot undergo or decline <u>hysterectomy</u>

* <u>Premenopausal</u> patients who want to preserve <u>fertility</u>

* Options

* <u>Levonorgestrel IUD</u> and/or continuous oral <u>progestin</u> (e.g., <u>megestrol acetate</u>, <u>medroxyprogesterone acetate</u>)

* There is no consensus on optimal dosing and duration of treatment; consult specialists.

* Follow-up (with treating specialist)

* <u>Endometrial sampling</u> within 3–6 months of treatment to assess response  [[2]](/library/wNdhWq0)[[10]](/library/IOdYFJ0)[[17]](/library/DNd1Wq0)

* Consider long-term <u>progestin</u> therapy for patients with ongoing <u>risk factors for endometrial cancer</u>. [[10]](/library/IOdYFJ0)

* Advise patients to promptly follow up with their treating physician if they experience abnormal <u>vaginal bleeding</u> during <u>conservative management</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Total <u>hysterectomy</u> is the definitive management for <u>EIN</u>. <u>Progestin</u> therapy is an alternative treatment option in select patients if concurrent <u>endometrial cancer</u> has been ruled out. [[10]](/library/IOdYFJ0)




### Prevention [[2]](/library/wNdhWq0)




* Screening for <u>endometrial hyperplasia</u> in asymptomatic individuals is not recommended.

* <u>Primary prevention</u> measures are the same for <u>endometrial cancer</u>; see “<u>Prevention of endometrial cancer</u>” for details.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Obesity</u> is a major potentially <u>modifiable risk factor</u> for <u>endometrial hyperplasia</u> and <u>endometrial cancer</u>. [[2]](/library/wNdhWq0)[[10]](/library/IOdYFJ0)




> [!WARNING]
> Do not prescribe unopposed <u>estrogen</u> to a patient with an intact <u>uterus</u>. [[18]](/library/rbXfE9)[[19]](/library/es1xFR0)

## Endometrial polyps

### Definition [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)[[21]](/library/jod_bI0)




* Focal overgrowth(s) of benign <u>endometrial</u> tissue

* Localized within the uterine wall, extends into the <u>uterine cavity</u>

* Can be <u>pedunculated</u> or <u>sessile</u>, single or multiple, and up to many centimeters in size

* May contain <u>smooth muscle cells</u> and/or <u>blood vessels</u>

* Expresses both <u>estrogen</u> and <u>progesterone</u> <u>receptors</u> (<u>estrogen</u> may stimulate growth)





### Etiology




The exact etiology is not clear. Risk factors for endometrial polyps include: [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)[[21]](/library/jod_bI0)




* <u>Hypertension</u>

* <u>Tamoxifen</u>

* Older age

* <u>Postmenopausal</u> status

* <u>Hyperestrogenic</u> conditions

* <u>Obesity</u>

* <u>PCOS</u>

* <u>Estrogen</u>-secreting <u>ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor</u>

* <u>Chronic liver disease</u>

* Late <u>menopause</u>

* <u>Hormone replacement therapy</u>  [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)





### Clinical features [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)[[22]](/library/yOddEJ0)




* Usually asymptomatic

* Symptoms in <u>premenopausal</u> individuals

* <u>Abnormal uterine bleeding</u> (most common symptom) [[21]](/library/jod_bI0)

* <u>Infertility</u>  [[23]](/library/BHXzsz)

* <u>Recurrent pregnancy loss</u>

* Symptoms in <u>postmenopausal</u> individuals: <u>postmenopausal bleeding</u> or spotting





### Diagnostics [[4]](/library/uEWpxM0)[[8]](/library/3yWSUL0)




See “<u>Diagnostics for AUB</u>,” “<u>Diagnostics for infertility</u>,” and “<u>Diagnostics for PMB</u>.” as needed.




* <u>TVUS</u> with <u>color Doppler ultrasound</u> ;  [[8]](/library/3yWSUL0)[[24]](/library/-x1D_Q0)

* First-line imaging for suspected <u>endometrial polyp</u>(s)

* Findings include: [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)[[25]](/library/0mdeVq0)

* Focal, homogeneous, echogenic <u>endometrial</u> mass with preserved <u>endometrial</u>-myometrial interface

* Distortion of the usual <u>endometrial</u> contour (interrupted <u>mucosa</u> sign)

* A single blood vessel supplying a polyp may be visible with <u>color Doppler ultrasound</u> [[8]](/library/3yWSUL0)

* Additional studies for inconclusive <u>TVUS</u> findings [[8]](/library/3yWSUL0)[[21]](/library/jod_bI0)

* <u>Hysteroscopy</u>  [[4]](/library/uEWpxM0)[[22]](/library/yOddEJ0)

* <u>Sonohysterography</u>  [[4]](/library/uEWpxM0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>MRI</u> <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast is not a routine imaging modality to evaluate for <u>endometrial polyps</u> but it may be considered if there is concern for <u>malignancy</u> or if transvaginal access (e.g., for <u>hysteroscopy</u>) is not feasible. [[4]](/library/uEWpxM0)[[8]](/library/3yWSUL0)[[24]](/library/-x1D_Q0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Blind endometrial biopsy</u> may rule out differential diagnoses (e.g., <u>endometrial hyperplasia</u>, <u>endometrial carcinoma</u>) but is not recommended for the evaluation of focal lesions of the <u>uterine cavity</u>, such as <u>endometrial polyps</u>. [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)[[21]](/library/jod_bI0)[[26]](/library/vIdAer0)




### Differential diagnoses




* <u>Endometrial hyperplasia</u>

* <u>Endometrial carcinoma</u>

* <u>Uterine leiomyoma</u>

* Other <u>causes of AUB</u>

* Other <u>causes of PMB</u>





### Treatment [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)[[21]](/library/jod_bI0)




Management is based on symptoms and <u>risk factors for malignant endometrial polyp(s)</u>.




#### Observation and follow-up




* Indicated in asymptomatic <u>premenopausal</u> patients without indications for polypectomy

* Consider repeat imaging in 6–12 months if <u>risk factors for type I endometrial cancer</u> develop.  [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)

* Spontaneous regression occurs in ∼ 25% of lesions; smaller lesions (≤ 1 cm) are more likely to regress. [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)





#### Hysteroscopic polypectomy




Referral to <u>OB/GYN</u> for consideration of polypectomy is indicated in the following situations.




* Patients with risk factors for malignant endometrial polyp(s), i.e.: [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)[[21]](/library/jod_bI0)

* <u>Premenopausal</u> patients with <u>AUB</u>

* <u>Postmenopausal</u> patients (with or without symptoms)

* <u>Tamoxifen</u> therapy

* Age ≥ 60 years

* <u>Risk factors for endometrial cancer</u>

* <u>Premenopausal</u> patients with <u>infertility</u> and/or <u>recurrent pregnancy loss</u>  [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)[[21]](/library/jod_bI0)[[22]](/library/yOddEJ0)

* Large polyps (e.g., ≥ 1 cm)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>AUB</u>, <u>postmenopausal</u> status, and <u>tamoxifen</u> use are the major <u>risk factors for malignant endometrial polyps</u>. [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)




> [!TIP]
> Hysteroscopic polypectomy is indicated in symptomatic <u>premenopausal</u> patients, all <u>postmenopausal</u> patients, and patients with other <u>risk factors</u> for <u>malignancy</u>. [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)[[21]](/library/jod_bI0)




### Prognosis [[20]](/library/nKd7SI0)




* ∼ 0.5–5% of <u>endometrial polyps</u> are premalignant or malignant.

* The risk increases with <u>menopause</u>, age ≥ 60 years, and/or <u>tamoxifen</u> use.
